                  <jats:p>
                    Pathogenic
                    <jats:italic>BRCA</jats:italic>
                    <jats:italic>1</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>BRCA2</jats:italic>
                    germline variants confer an increased risk of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC). In this high-risk cohort, novel biomarkers are needed to support patient management. While circulating cell-free DNA-based conventional CpG-level averaging is promising, it dilutes tumor-specific signals in samples with low circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) fractions. Here, we developed a targeted ultra-deep NGS assay for detecting tumor-derived ctDNA based on fragment-level hypermethylation of CpG-rich cfDNA. A panel of 360 cancer-specific CpG-rich regions derived from 450k methylation array datasets from TCGA breast cancer and GEO ovarian cancer, was applied to plasma from 31 breast cancer, 16 ovarian cancer patients, and 26 healthy controls using enzymatic methylation sequencing. Hypermethylated ctDNA (hm-ctDNA) fragments, were significantly enriched in cancer cases, identifying 62.5% of ovarian and 38.7% of breast cancers at 100% specificity. Elevated hm-ctDNA was observed across different tumor stages, with higher burden in
                    <jats:italic>BRCA</jats:italic>
                    <jats:italic>1</jats:italic>
                    -associated cases. This approach enables highly specific, non-invasive hypermethylated ctDNA detection in HBOC populations.
                  </jats:p>
title: Hypermethylation in CpG-rich cfDNA fragments enables accurate detection of circulating tumor DNA in BRCA1- and BRCA2-associated breast and ovarian cancer

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Titanium alloy powders are susceptible to oxygen pickup during handling, storage, and usage in additive manufacturing (AM), which degrades the 3D-printed parts’ mechanical properties and severely limits their reuse. Industrial AM titanium alloy feedstocks are subjected to stringent oxygen requirements, leading to large volumes of high-oxygen powder waste, which increases carbon footprint and cost. Thermochemical reduction with strong oxygen-affinity metals offers a viable route for titanium powder recovery, yet the oxygen removal mechanism from powder surfaces remains to be confirmed by direct experimental observation. Here, calciothermic reduction of AM-grade spherical Ti-6Al-4V powder is performed, followed by acid pickling and drying. Multiscale characterization is employed to correlate changes in bulk oxygen content, surface morphology, oxide-layer structure, and near-surface chemistry at the individual-particle level. Atom probe tomography reveals a graded oxygen profile extending from a TiO₂ outer surface through progressively oxygen-depleted subsurface regions into the α-Ti64 matrix. The oxidized and rejuvenated powders exhibit oxide regions of approximately 10 and <5 nm, respectively, while the matrix oxygen concentration decreased from about 3.2 to 0.5 at.%. A Ca–O-rich reaction-product layer and a narrow Ca–Ti–O interfacial region were directly observed after reduction, indicating that oxygen transfer occurs through a surface-mediated interfacial reaction.</jats:p>
title: Direct observation of surface chemistry evolution for Ti-6Al-4V powders in calciothermic reduction recycling process

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fatigue is a common, multidimensional symptom in cancer patients. Little is known about fatigue dimensions and their trajectories in prostate cancer (PCa).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI), 1097 men treated with radiotherapy for non-metastatic PCa (2014–2016) prospectively reported fatigue up to five years later. Prevalent fatigue was defined as scores ≥75th percentile in men aged ≥60 years in a German general population sample. Pre-radiotherapy patient characteristics were examined for their associations with general fatigue, physical fatigue, mental fatigue, reduced activity, and reduced motivation two years later using logistic regression models. Fatigue trajectories up to two years post-radiotherapy were explored using latent class growth analysis and multinomial regression.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>About 72% (785/1097) of patients reported being fatigued for at least one dimension in the MFI from before the start of radiotherapy up to five years later, with 45% (367/816) being fatigued two years post-radiotherapy. Pre-radiotherapy fatigue level (OR: 4.7–9.0), depression (OR: 2.5), diabetes (OR: 1.8–2.2), hypertension (OR: 1.6–1.8), and BMI (OR: 1.8–2.2) were statistically significant predictors of long-term fatigue two years post-radiotherapy across dimensions. Depression, BMI, and pelvic radiotherapy were associated with experiencing a high fatigue trajectory.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Early fatigue assessments, in addition to self-reported comorbidities and BMI, showed additional benefits beyond symptom detection by providing prognostic value for poorer long-term fatigue outcomes. Multidimensional fatigue assessments could guide tailored symptom management strategies, targeting specific dimensions to address associated impairments in quality of life and functioning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Long-term fatigue dimensions in the Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory (MFI) up to five years after radiotherapy and their trajectories in men diagnosed with non-metastatic prostate cancer in the international REQUITE study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Corrosion of structural alloys remains a critical challenge for advanced molten salt reactors, where aggressive fluoride salts promote continuous dissolution at the salt–metal interface. While most mitigation strategies emphasize thermodynamic stability, kinetic control of atomic transport has received comparatively less attention. Here, we propose a corrosion mitigation strategy based on diffusion control and vacancy trapping by dilute yttrium (Y) solutes and yttrium oxide (Y
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    ) dispersions in Ni alloys. A combined computational and experimental approach integrates density functional theory (DFT), self-consistent mean-field (SCMF) diffusion modeling, and an impurity trapping model to quantify the impact of defect trapping on effective vacancy mobility. Strong first-nearest-neighbor vacancy–Y binding, off-lattice vacancy configurations, and elevated rotational and dissociation barriers result in pronounced suppression of vacancy diffusivity, while Y
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    -associated sites treated as fixed traps in the model further reduce the mobile vacancy population. Ni–Mo (NM), Y-modified (NMY), and Y
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    O
                    <jats:sub>3</jats:sub>
                    -containing (NMYO) alloys were tested in molten fluoride salt at 750 
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    C. Corrosion penetration decreases systematically from NM to NMY to NMYO, consistent with the predicted reduction in vacancy-mediated transport. The same trend is observed in mass change, with net weight loss decreasing from 0.52% for NM to 0.23% for NMY and 0.09% for NMYO. These results are consistent with an alloy-side transport contribution from defect trapping and reduced atomic transport. This study therefore suggests point defect engineering as a promising alloy design strategy for extreme nuclear environments.
                  </jats:p>
title: Role of defect trapping in the enhanced corrosion resistance of Ni–Mo alloys with yttrium and yttrium oxide additions

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Genomic instability is associated with breast cancer immune response. We sought to evaluate joint effects of genomic instability and immune response on recurrence using validated RNA-based assays and statistical models for assessing joint expression in a population-based dataset (
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                     = 2783). Prognostic value of the resulting coordinated signature, Repair, Immune, and Genomics for Oncologic Reclassification (RIGOR150), was assessed in estrogen receptor (ER)+ and ER− breast cancers (
                    <jats:italic>N</jats:italic>
                     = 1899 with recurrence information) and validated in public datasets. RIGOR150 was strongly associated with recurrence risk in training (Hazard Ratio [HR] for high vs. low-risk = 5.10, 95% confidence interval [CI] = 3.19, 8.15) and test data (HR = 3.07, 95% CI = 1.73, 5.45) and was validated in external datasets. Among ER+ tumors, RIGOR150 high-risk was associated with early (0–5 years, HR = 5.75, 95% CI = 3.38, 9.77) and late recurrence (5–10 years, HR = 2.67, 95% CI = 1.26, 5.65). RIGOR150 added prognostic value independent of existing risk predictors (21-gene recurrence score and PAM50), and was associated with neoantigens, proliferation, and tumor-immune cell proximity. Overall, joint patterns of genomic instability and immunogenicity augment current breast cancer prognostic scores, providing early and late prognostication.
                  </jats:p>
title: Coordinated patterns of genomic instability and immunogenicity predict 10-year breast cancer progression across subtypes and patient characteristics
